name: The Institutional Theory of Art
statement: Something is art not because of how it looks but because the artworld confers that status on it.
statementAccent: because the artworld confers that status
meaning: The institutional theory of art defines art not by any intrinsic, manifest, or exhibited property, such as beauty, representation, or form, but relationally, by an artwork's relation to the social institution of the artworld. It arose as a response to Weitz's anti-essentialism and to avant-garde works, like Duchamp's readymades, that count as art yet share no common visible feature with traditional works. The philosopher Arthur Danto introduced the term artworld in his 1964 paper The Artworld, arguing that to see something as art requires something the eye cannot descry, an atmosphere of artistic theory, a knowledge of the history of art, an artworld; his example was Andy Warhol's Brillo Box, perceptually indistinguishable from ordinary supermarket cartons, so that what makes it art is not a visible property but its embedding in a theory and history. Danto inspired rather than proposed the institutional theory; his own later view is historical and interpretive. George Dickie developed the institutional theory proper. In his 1974 book Art and the Aesthetic, he defined a work of art as, first, an artifact, and second, a set of the aspects of which has had conferred upon it the status of candidate for appreciation by some person acting on behalf of a certain social institution, the artworld. In his 1984 book The Art Circle he revised this into a set of interrelated definitions of artist, work, public, artworld system, and artworld, often criticized as circular.
mechanism: The institutional theory relocates the ground of arthood from a work's perceptible qualities to its standing within a practice. The motivating observation, dramatized by Danto with Warhol's Brillo Box, is that two objects can be perceptually identical while one is art and the other is not, so no exhibited property can be what makes something art; the difference lies in an invisible relation to a background of theory, history, and institutions, the artworld. Dickie made this into a definition. On his classificatory account, being a work of art requires two things: being an artifact, something made or adapted, and having had conferred upon it, by a person acting on behalf of the artworld, the status of candidate for appreciation. The conferral is like other institutional acts, such as knighting or christening, in which a person with the appropriate standing, by acting within an established practice, changes the status of something without changing its physical properties; a urinal becomes a candidate for appreciation when placed by an artist within the artworld in the right way. This explains how readymades and conceptual works, which lack any common look, can all be art: they are all objects on which the artworld has conferred the relevant status. Dickie's later Art Circle version defines the key notions, artist, artwork, public, artworld system, and artworld, in terms of one another, an interlocking or circular set of definitions that he defended as informatively describing the practice even though it is not reductive. Throughout, the theory makes arthood a matter of social and relational context rather than of manifest features.

examples.text: Danto argued that seeing something as art requires an atmosphere of theory and a knowledge of art history, an artworld.
Warhol's Brillo Box is indistinguishable from supermarket cartons, so its arthood lies not in its look but in its context.
For Dickie, an artwork is an artifact on which someone acting for the artworld confers the status of candidate for appreciation.

whyItMatters: The institutional theory of art is one of the most influential responses to the crisis that modern and conceptual art created for the definition of art. Once artists could present readymades, indistinguishable industrial objects, and purely conceptual gestures as art, no definition in terms of beauty, representation, or form could survive, and Weitz had argued that art could not be defined at all. The institutional theory offered a way to define art after all, by shifting the focus from a work's perceptible properties to its relations to a social practice, the artworld, and it thereby made sense of exactly the hard cases that broke the classical theories. Danto's insight that perceptually identical objects can differ in art status, and Dickie's account of arthood as conferred within an institution, reoriented the philosophy of art toward the social and historical context of art-making and reception. The theory has been enormously discussed, both for its explanatory power over avant-garde art and for its notorious difficulties, above all the charge of circularity and the worry that it makes arthood a matter of mere fiat. Whether accepted or rejected, it is a landmark in the definition-of-art debate. As the view that art is what the artworld makes art, the institutional theory is a central position in aesthetics.

working.text: recognize that perceptually identical objects can differ in art status, so no visible feature defines art.
locate arthood in a work's relation to the artworld, a background of theory, history, and practice.
count as art an artifact on which someone acting for the artworld has conferred the status of candidate for appreciation.

limits: The institutional theory faces serious objections, the most famous being circularity. Because it defines a work of art in terms of the artworld, and the artworld in terms of art, artists, and artworks, the definition appears to explain art by presupposing it, and Dickie's Art Circle version, with its interlocking definitions, makes this circle explicit; Dickie argued the circularity is informative rather than vicious, but critics disagree. The theory is also charged with saying too little: it does not explain what confers the status of art, or why anyone would confer it, and it seems to allow that anyone with the right institutional standing could make anything art by fiat, without regard to the object's merit, so that the theory cannot distinguish good art from bad or say what the artworld is for. It struggles with art made outside any institution, such as prehistoric cave paintings or art from cultures with no artworld in the relevant sense. Danto himself did not endorse the institutional theory as a definition, holding instead a historical and interpretive view. Some details reward care: Danto's paper is dated 1964 and Dickie's books 1974 and 1984, and the relevant IEP coverage appears under a Definition of Art or Aesthetics entry. So the institutional theory robustly makes arthood a matter of conferred institutional status, understood as an influential account beset by circularity and by the worry that it reduces art to fiat.
misreadings: The institutional theory does not say that art has no perceptible qualities, only that arthood is fixed by relations to the artworld rather than by those qualities. It does not claim that anyone at all can make something art, but that someone acting on behalf of the artworld can confer the relevant status. And Danto, who coined artworld, did not himself propose the institutional theory as a definition, holding a different, historical view, so treating the theory as denying that artworks have features, as licensing arthood by anyone, or as Danto's own definition, misreads it.
origin: George Dickie's definition of art, inspired by Arthur Danto's 1964 notion of the artworld, that a work of art is an artifact on which someone acting for the artworld has conferred the status of candidate for appreciation.
